title: The single-expression implication for identities of $f(x,y)=x^2+y^3$
statement: Let $f(x,y)=x^2+y^3$. An **expression** is formed by recursively applying $f$ to a set of variables. Suppose that $G(x)$ is an expression formed by recursively applying $f$ to the variable set $\{x\}$, with variable positions $v_1,\ldots,v_l$. For a positive integer $n$ and variables $\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$, let $G(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ be obtained by assigning each variable position $v_i$ one of the variables $x_1,\ldots,x_n$. A **nontrivial identity** is an equality between two distinct expressions that holds as a polynomial identity over $\mathbb{R}$. **The single-expression implication.** If $G(x)$ cannot occur as either side of a nontrivial one-variable identity, then $G(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ cannot occur as either side of a nontrivial $n$-variable identity.
